liston.name: Melba Liston

he_said.summary: Weston said only Melba Liston could arrange “Spirit of Our Ancestors”, told how he goaded her back to work after her stroke — she learned to write music on a computer with her left hand — and recalled her arrangements arriving from a California hospital in time for the 1959 Five Spot date and the 1985 Montreal concert.
he_said.one_liner: his arranger; wrote left-handed after her stroke
he_said.his_quote: I went to see her, and I insulted her as only musicians can do. I called her all kinds of names. I said to her, “You have to do these arrangements stroke or no stroke, handicap or no handicap,” you know? She cried a little bit, you know?

more_his_quotes.quote: Then I realized that only Melba Liston could do this.
Well, it was her genius and her strength, and her spiritual strength.
Spirit. It makes no difference where she was: North Pole, or the middle of the Congo, it makes no difference.
She was in the hospital in California, and by some miracle the music arrived the day of the recording.

he_said.notes: Jenkins supplies 'such a long partnership'. Weston says Melba 'can no longer play the trombone'.

albums_together: Live at the Five Spot (Randy Weston album)

they_said.summary: Liston said she met Randy Weston while playing with Dizzy Gillespie at Birdland, arranged his music (including Little Niles) for some forty years with complete freedom, and credited him with pulling her through after her stroke when nobody else stuck with her.
they_said.her_quote: I’ve been writing for Randy. I’m still writing for Randy. I wrote for him up until I had the stroke. After I had the stroke and got over a little bit, I’m writing for him again. I think he pulled me out of it – helped anyway. I thank him very much for sticking with me, because nobody else did.

more_her_quotes.quote: He stayed over and met me when I finished the gig. He said, “I have to meet her.” We just hit it off right away.
He brought Little Niles and all those things up to the house, and he said, “I think you should write these things for an album for me.” And I wrote them. I think it’s the best thing.
But we’ve been together – what? – ’56 to ’96. How many is that? 40 years. He don’t tell me anything.
He says I write like he writes.

they_said.notes: Many further Liston lines: 295713 ('He took me to Jamaica.'), 295899 ('Randy, I have all the freedom I want.'), 295937 ('Randy pulled me out of the stroke, so I have to go with him.'), 296190 ('Randy likes Thelonious much.'), 296393/296397 (helped her start writing again after the stroke). Bryant's narration of the recordings (Little Niles 1956/1973 Tanjah/Earth Birth, Hi-Fly) is hers, not Liston's.

weston_as_her_witness.one_liner: relied on her arrangements, even after her stroke
weston_as_her_witness.summary: Weston said only Liston could arrange 'Spirit of Our Ancestors', told how he goaded her back to work after the stroke that left her unable to play, after which she learned to write music by computer with her left hand, and praised her genius and spiritual strength through years of illness.
weston_as_her_witness.lead_quote: Then I realized that only Melba Liston could do this.
weston_as_her_witness.second_quote: Unfortunately, she has had problems with illness. But, her spiritual strength is so powerful.
weston_as_her_witness.caution: The stroke anecdote includes 'I insulted her as only musicians can do. I called her all kinds of names' and 'She cried a little bit' -- affectionate goading in context, but harsh if excerpted; avoid quoting those lines alone. Dates are Weston's recollection: he places the Hawkins Five Spot date in 1959 and the Montreal festival concert in 1985, while the interviewer dates the Montreal residency to '97 -- check against the discography. The interviewer's 'long partnership' phrase is hers, not his.

liston_as_his_witness.one_liner: wrote his arrangements for forty years
liston_as_his_witness.summary: Liston recalled meeting Weston while playing with Dizzy Gillespie, said she had arranged his music with complete freedom from ’56 to ’96, and thanked him for pulling her through after her stroke when nobody else stuck with her.
liston_as_his_witness.lead_quote: I wrote for him up until I had the stroke. After I had the stroke and got over a little bit, I’m writing for him again. I think he pulled me out of it – helped anyway. I thank him very much for sticking with me, because nobody else did.
liston_as_his_witness.second_quote: He brought Little Niles and all those things up to the house, and he said, “I think you should write these things for an album for me.” And I wrote them. I think it’s the best thing.
liston_as_his_witness.caution: 'because nobody else did' is her view after the stroke; in the next turn she names Frank and other arrangers as friends, so it should not be read as an accusation against named people. Many Weston lines in this interview are the interviewer Clora Bryant's ('Randy is your horn right now', the recording dates, 'in different clothing') and must not be attributed to Liston. '[Weston]' in 'Randy [Weston]' is the transcriber's bracket. 'He don’t tell me anything' (295901) means he gives her free rein, not that he is uncommunicative; do not show it without the freedom context.
